title: Final review week
intro: Use this plan in the last 7 days before CIA Part 1, after you have worked through the notes and taken your mocks. Nothing in it is new: the week sharpens what you already know. Most days take about an hour; the two mock days take longer.
how_it_works: No new topics this week. Late new material crowds out what you have already learned.
One full timed mock at the start of the week, then no more full mocks. The last days are for recall and rest.
Answer from memory first, then check. Recalling builds memory; rereading mostly makes pages feel familiar.
Time follows the exam weights, so Sections A and C, together about two thirds of the exam, get the most.
Part 1 turns on close pairs: must or should, function or person, approve or consult. A few minutes a day on these pairs keeps them apart.
Memory settles while you sleep, so a full night's rest is part of the plan. Missed a day? Skip it and carry on; never double up.

days.title: Full rehearsal
days.goal: Sit one full timed mock at the real length, ideally at your exam's start time, to rehearse pace and stamina.

tasks.text: Take a full timed mock in one sitting: 125 questions in 150 minutes, phone away, no notes.
Pace by two checkpoints, not by timing each question: question 50 by minute 60; question 100 by minute 120.
Stuck on one? Choose your best answer, flag it and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized on the real exam.
Your misses go to your mistake journal on their own. Rest tonight and review them tomorrow.

days.remember: A mock is a rehearsal, not a verdict. KaiSip shows percent by section; that is not The IIA's scaled score and cannot predict your result.

days.title: Learn from your misses
days.goal: Trace each mock miss to its thinking slip, then recall the two heaviest sections. Stop at about 90 minutes.

tasks.text: In your mistake journal, review each miss from the mock, newest first.
Tag why you missed each one: “Acted as the wrong person”, “Missed ‘first’ or ‘best’”, “Tool before policy”, “Fixed the symptom, not the cause”, “Misread” or “Didn’t know it”.
Read the principles behind the slip you tagged most often.
From memory, list three Section A and three Section C points. Then open the lists and check.
Read the principles on your seat: who acts, who approves and who owns the fix.

days.remember: A miss you understand is worth more than a right answer you guessed.

days.title: The three close pairs
days.goal: Drill the pairs Part 1 turns on, recall Section B, and work on the section furthest behind its weight.

tasks.text: Must or should: without looking, name one yearly duty that is a requirement and one that is good practice. Then check the principle.
Function or person: name one threat to independence and one to objectivity, and say who hears about each. Then check the principles on staying unbiased.
Approve or consult: say who approves the charter, the plan and the budget, and who gives input only. Then check the note.
From memory, list three Section B points. Then open the list and check.
Answer a short untimed set in your focus section. Before each answer, name the actor in the question.

days.remember: A must is a requirement; a should is good practice. The board approves; senior management gives input.

days.title: Pace check
days.goal: Keep your pace sharp with one short timed mock, then recall how risk drives the work and what makes a conclusion hold.

tasks.text: Take the short timed mock in one sitting. Watch your pace more than the score.
Without looking, say what has to be settled before any testing starts. Then check the principles on what drives the work.
From memory, explain risk appetite and risk tolerance, and who hears when accepted risk goes above them. Then check the note.
Read the principles on proving it: evidence, root cause and what assurance cannot promise.

days.remember: This is your last timed test before the exam. From here, short recall keeps you sharp.

days.title: Fraud risks and speaking up
days.goal: Recall Section D from the internal auditor's seat, sharpen how you read questions, and work on your second gap.

tasks.text: From memory, list three Section D points and say who acts in each. Then open the list and check.
Read the principles on speaking up: the right channel, the right order and the plain truth.
Read the principles on reading the question.
Practice a short untimed set in your second-weakest section. Find the priority word before you read the options.
Redo your mistake journal questions. Before you choose, say why your old answer loses.

days.remember: The internal auditor considers fraud risk and reports concerns. Deciding that fraud took place is for an investigation.

days.title: Light review and logistics
days.goal: Touch everything once, lightly, and settle the practical details so nothing on the day is a surprise.

tasks.text: For each section, recall two points before you open its list, starting with Section A. Spend a few minutes, not an hour.
Say the seven priority words and the answering steps from memory, then check them.
Say the three pairs once more: must or should, function or person, approve or consult. Then glance at the one-line rules.
Look up any term on the lists that still feels fuzzy.
Confirm your appointment, the test center's address and your route. Read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's candidate handbook.

days.remember: Recall beats rereading. Leave new material alone now.

days.title: The eve
days.goal: Stay fresh, not tired: a light touch in the morning, then rest.

tasks.text: Optional: say the answering steps and your two checkpoints from memory, then check them. Stop after 15 minutes.
Read the one-line rule for your most common slip on the principles list.
Work through the eve checklist.
Close the books by early evening and keep your usual bedtime.

days.remember: Rest is part of the plan. If sleep comes slowly tonight, that is common, and your preparation is already done.

eve: Your appointment is confirmed, and you have read the ID and check-in rules in The IIA's current candidate handbook.
Your route to the test center and your travel time are planned, with a backup.
Your ID is laid out where you will see it in the morning.
You have read the reminder for your most common slip.
Skip alcohol tonight; it makes sleep lighter.
If worries keep circling, write them down for a few minutes, then put the page away.
Books are closed by early evening, and you keep your usual bedtime.
morning: Eat a familiar breakfast and keep your usual caffeine.
Reread your two checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 100 by minute 120.
Leave early enough that a delay on the way would not matter.
Remind yourself of your seat: an internal auditor who assesses, advises and reports, while management owns the risk and the fix.
A racing heart is your body getting ready. Treat it as energy for focus, not a sign of danger.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and move on.

points.text: Purpose: internal auditing gives the board and management independent, objective, risk-based assurance, advice, insight and foresight. Managing risk, running controls and deciding stay with management.
Approve or consult: the chief audit executive drafts and discusses; the board alone approves the charter, the internal audit plan and the budget. Senior management gives input and support.

A charter must state at least four things: the Purpose of Internal Auditing, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate with scope and services, and the function's position and reporting relationships.

Assurance means criteria, evidence and a conclusion. Advisory work is advice without assurance, with its scope agreed with the requesting party. The Standards apply to both: management makes every decision, and a significant risk is still reported as a finding.

Independence is the function's and rests on a direct line to the board. The chief audit executive must confirm it to the board at least yearly. An administrative line to the chief executive officer is a leading practice.

In an engagement, a scope limitation or restricted access is discussed with management; if unresolved, the chief audit executive must elevate it to the board. A cut to board-approved scope or budget goes promptly to the board and senior management.

Three Lines Model: first-line management owns and manages risk; second-line roles support, monitor and challenge; internal audit, the third line, gives independent assurance and advice and never owns what it later assesses.
Honesty and professional courage: report what the evidence shows, in full and with respect. Pressure, friendship or fear never justifies softening, delaying or dropping a finding.
Objectivity is the person's unbiased mindset. A conflict of interest counts in fact or in appearance, so your own confidence does not settle it.

Never assess an activity you were responsible for. For assurance, objectivity is presumed impaired if that responsibility ended within the previous 12 months. Advisory work on it is allowed after disclosure to the requesting party.

Disclose an impairment promptly: the auditor to the chief audit executive or a designated supervisor, the chief audit executive's own to the board. The chief audit executive decides the safeguard; the options are not ranked.
Refuse any gift, reward or favor that could impair objectivity, or could be presumed to, whatever its value.
Take on only work you have, or can obtain, the competencies for. Due professional care is reasonable care, not a guarantee; skepticism questions the information, not the person.
Use information only for the work and share it only with people authorized to receive it. Confidentiality never keeps a finding from the board.

The board directs and oversees; management runs the organization and owns its risks and controls; internal audit assures and advises. An option that hands internal audit a decision, a policy or a risk is wrong.
Judge the control environment by what leaders do and reward, not by the policy manual alone. A weak tone at the top weakens every control beneath it.

Inherent risk is the risk before management's actions. Residual risk is what remains after what management has done, not after what the auditor recommends, and it is compared with appetite and tolerance.
Risk appetite is how much risk, of what kinds, the organization will take. Risk tolerance is the acceptable variation around an objective. Internal audit measures against both and sets neither.

Management chooses the risk response. If accepted risk is above appetite or tolerance, the chief audit executive discusses it with senior management, then escalates to the board if unresolved. Resolving it is not the chief audit executive's job.

Classify a control by what it does: preventive stops the event, detective reveals it afterward, corrective repairs it, directive tells people what is expected. A reconciliation or a review is detective, however often it runs.
Two control questions: would it work if done (design), and is it done (operation)? A design gap is a finding in its own right. Controls give reasonable assurance, never absolute assurance.
Fraud needs intent; error does not. The fraud triangle has three sides: opportunity, motivation (pressure) and rationalization. Segregation of duties, approvals and reviews reduce opportunity.
Considering fraud risk in every engagement risk assessment, during planning, is a must. Only when management asks, only in a fraud audit and only after testing are all wrong.
Exposure is judged from value, access, pressure and weak oversight, not from the size of a department or a clean record.
Management owns fraud risk management and the board oversees it. Internal audit evaluates and advises, and its plan must consider coverage of fraud risk.
A red flag starts work; it does not prove fraud. Corroborate it with independent evidence, then report through the channel that policy and law set. Never hide a finding.
Segregation of duties and approval limits prevent; reconciliations, supervisory reviews and hotlines detect. A detective control done by the person whose work it checks is not operating.
Investigations: internal audit's part depends on its mandate and on having, or obtaining, the competencies. It does not lead an investigation by default.

principles.intro: The mindset principles, one line each. Read a few a day this week, starting with the family behind your most common slip.

priority_words.meaning: Order. What must happen before anything else? Usually understanding and planning come before testing, discussion before escalation, and disclosure before a safeguard.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what does everything else depend on?

priority_words.meaning: Several options would help. Pick the one that fits the internal auditor's seat: it assesses, advises or reports, reaches the cause, and leaves the decision with its owner.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one keeps me in my seat?

priority_words.meaning: A ranking on one named quality, such as most reliable, most important or most appropriate. Judge the options on that quality only.
The main purpose or reason, not a side benefit. The charter exists to state the mandate and the function's position; a reporting line to the board exists to protect independence.
priority_words.cue: Ask: why does this exist at all?

priority_words.meaning: The largest amount of the named quality. For a risk or a threat, weigh likelihood and impact together and look for the widest effect on the organization's objectives.
priority_words.cue: Ask: greatest what, and for which objective?

priority_words.meaning: Probability, not severity. What is most probable from the facts given, even if another outcome would be worse.
priority_words.cue: Ask: what usually follows from these facts?

priority_words.meaning: Rare on CIA questions, which usually ask for the right answer. If you meet it, flip the test: three options fit, and you want the one that fits least. Slow down.
priority_words.cue: Ask: which one does not belong?

answering_routine.title: Read the last line first
answering_routine.text: Find what is asked: an action, a person, a document, a rule or a reason.

answering_routine.title: Find the actor and the priority word
answering_routine.text: Who is acting: an internal auditor, the chief audit executive, the board or management? Then find the priority word, written in lowercase, such as “first”, “best”, “most”, “primary” or “most likely”, before you read the options.

answering_routine.title: Check the strength and the facts
answering_routine.text: Does the question ask what is required, or what is good practice? Note words such as already, approved, unresolved, assurance or advisory.

answering_routine.title: Eliminate two
answering_routine.text: Strike options where the auditor decides or fixes for management, senior management approves, a step is skipped, or a should is called a must.

answering_routine.title: Settle the final two with a principle
answering_routine.text: Ask who owns the decision, function or person, what comes first, and which option reaches the cause. Say the reason in one sentence, then answer.

pace: 125 questions in 150 minutes is 1.2 minutes each. Use that to set checkpoints, not to time each question.
Checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 100 by minute 120. Look at the clock there and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? Those minutes are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few; do not rush them all.
Stuck? Choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so never leave a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one.
Change an answer when you find a clear reason, such as an actor or a priority word you missed the first time.
